question.text: After returning to England following the Munich Agreement, Chamberlain gave a speech in front of the Heston Aerodrome in which he uttered this infamously ironic four-word phrase which he believed he had achieved.
question.answerHtml: “ peace for our time ” (do not accept “peace in our time”)
question.clue: Upon returning from Munich, Chamberlain used this four word phrase to summarize the agreement. Apparently, Hitler did not agree, referring to the agreement as "a scrap of paper" before invading Poland.

swap.text: Three of Henry's wives shared this first name. Henry's first wife, a princess of Aragon, had this name, as did two wives from the Parr and Howard families.
swap.answerHtml: Catherine [accept Catherine of Aragon or Catherine Parr or Catherine Howard]
swap.clue: That person with this name was the widow of Arthur, Prince of Wales.

question.leadin: The last phase of the French Wars of religion were named for three people that bore this name.
question.text: Give this first name, which was beared by The Duke of Navarre, the Duke of Guise, and the King of France at that time. A King of England with six wives also had this name.
question.clue: An event known as the Day of the Barricades occurred during a war fought between three men with this name.

swap.text: This radical secret society of textile workers destroyed looms and other machines that were replacing them in England in the 1810s. Its name is used today for anyone resistant to technological change.
swap.clue: Like the Swing Riots, this movement was inspired by a mythological king or general.

question.text: In response to Jacques Delors' proposals for European integration, this British prime minister said "No. No. No." This Conservative was succeeded by John Major, who pulled the UᐧK out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism.
question.answerHtml: Margaret Thatcher [or Margaret Hilda Thatcher, Baroness Thatcher; prompt on Iron Lady]
question.clue: Newsweek Magazine ran the headline "The Empire Strikes Back" to describe this leader's response during a conflict in which the H.M.S. Sheffield was sunk by an Exocet missile.

swap.text: Critiquing the geographic breadth of older studies, Pomeranz preferred a comparison between China's highly-commercialized Yangtze Delta and this country where the Industrial Revolution first took place.
swap.answerHtml: Great Britain [or England or the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or UK or Kingdom of Great Britain]
swap.clue: This country launched two failed invasions of Buenos Aires in 1806 and 1807, and this country's namesake "legions" played critical roles in the battles of Boyaca and Carabobo.

question.leadin: His time as prime minister saw territorial conflicts with Spain in the Nootka Crisis.
question.text: Name this British prime minister from 1804 to 1806 who saw Britain join the Third Coalition. He was the youngest British prime minister ever.
question.clue: This man supported George III, but fell out with him over the issue of Catholic Emancipation after passing the Act of Union, so he resigned.

swap.text: This battle which saw Harold Godwinson emerge victorious is considered the end of the Viking Age. A legend states that at this battle a Viking warrior held off the entire Anglo-Saxon army.
swap.clue: According to legend, a single soldier held up one side's advance across a bridge over the Derwent River until an English soldier speared him from under the bridge.

question.leadin: John Milton refuted a book attributed to this author point-by-point in Eikonoklastes.
question.text: Name this author who allegedly wrote the pious diary Eikon Basilike. This ruler's death was preceded by Pride's Purge, in which some members of Parliament were blocked from entering the House of Commons.
question.answerHtml: Charles I [or Charles Stuart; prompt on Charles; prompt on Stuart]
question.clue: This ruler was depicted "at the hunt" by his court painter, Anthony van Dyck.

swap.leadin: Name these restrictive laws from British history.
swap.text: Richard Cobden and John Bright founded a namesake League to campaign against these laws that restricted the importation of foreign grain and are blamed for contributing to the Irish Potato Famine.
swap.clue: Early opposition to these acts was organized by James Wilson's founding of the magazine The Economist.

question.text: This cousin of Drake was one of the three commanders of the English fleet during the Armada, but is better known for being the first English merchant to take part in the Triangle Trade of slaves across the Atlantic.
question.clue: This commander of the Jesus of Lubeck and the Victory, the first English slave trader. He was also a Vice Admiral in the fleet that stopped the Spanish Armada.

swap.text: This advisor to Henry, the successor to Cardinal Wolsey, oversaw the dissolution of the monasteries. After Henry discovered that Anne of Cleves was ugly, he had this man executed for suggesting their marriage.
swap.clue: According to the Spanish Chronicle, he tortured a musician named Mark Smeaton in order to force him to confess to adultery.

question.leadin: They were the most radical faction of the Convenanters, who had come together in 1638 to keep Charles I of England from interfering in the Presbyterian Church of Scotland.
question.text: Name this group which became embroiled in the English Civil War as part of a scheme to convert Charles II to Presbyterianism and spread their religion to the whole of Britain.

swap.leadin: Traditions including the "wooden horse", which entailed tying a criminal to a wooden frame and parading around the village, inspired these events.
swap.text: Name these 1839-1843 riots during which farmers dressed up as its namesake women and destroyed toll-gates to protest unfair taxation.
swap.clue: Thomas Bullin's tax raises along roads in Wales led to these riots in which poor Welsh men cross-dressed and destroyed toll-gates.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about Catholics in England.
question.text: Passed under the reign of the notably Catholic James II, this piece of legislation forbade any person from holding a governmental or military office without first swearing that they did not believe in transubstantiation.
question.clue: Under this 1673 law, receipt of communion in the Church of England was a prerequisite to holding office. It remained in effect until 1828.

swap.leadin: In the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, this event is presaged by "excessive whirlwinds" and "fiery dragons."
swap.text: Name this 793 event in which Danish raiders arrived at a monastery and made off with the relics of St. Cuthbert.

question.text: This 1866 novel was the last to be finished by Kingsley, and depicts an outlaw who was defeated at Ely after leading a revolt against William the Conqueror.
question.clue: This English outlaw who roamed the Fens. This person's namesake Gesta states that they returned to England from exile in Flanders to discover their brother's murder at the hands of the Normans.

swap.text: The Reform Act of 1832 was passed while this Whig served as Home Secretary. He would become Prime Minister in 1834.

question.leadin: Originally home to the Ordovices and Cornovii, this Welsh kingdom was ruled by the House of Gwerthynion until the 12th century.
question.text: Allegedly ruled by the descendants of Magnus Maximus, this kingdom apexed under Rhodri the Great. Described as a utopia, it was later divided into Fadog and Wen-wyn-wyn after the death of Madog ap Maredudd.

swap.text: Sands was held in this prison during his hunger strike, during which he was elected to parliament as a member of its anti-H block group. Liam Averill escaped from here by dressing up as a woman during a Christmas party.
